claim: Mice achieved 86 ± 9% correct choices (mean ± sd) on trials with single high-contrast gratings.
source: Mice became proficient in the task, achieving 86 ± 9% correct choices (mean ± sd) on trials with single high-contrast gratings, and the probability of their choices varied with the contrasts of the two gratings (Figure 1e–h).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific performance data (86 ± 9% correct choices) measured during the behavioral task.

claim: In the absence of visual stimuli, mice correctly held the wheel still (NoGo) in 54 ± 16% of the trials.
source: In the absence of visual stimuli, moreover, mice correctly held the wheel still (NoGo) in 54 ± 16% of the trials.
evidence: The manuscript reports specific behavioral data (54 ± 16% NoGo trials) measured during the task.

claim: When a stimulus was present, mice could err with a NoGo (a 'Miss' trial, 16 ± 13% of all trials where a stimulus was present on one side).
source: When a stimulus was present, mice could err with a NoGo (a 'Miss' trial, 16 ± 13% of all trials where a stimulus was present on one side, mean ± sd across sessions) or with a wheel turn in the incorrect direction ('Incorrect choice,' 7 ± 4%).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific error rate data (16 ± 13% Miss trials) measured during the task.

claim: Mice could err with a wheel turn in the incorrect direction ('Incorrect choice,' 7 ± 4%).

evidence: The manuscript reports specific error rate data (7 ± 4% Incorrect choices) measured during the task.

claim: The probability of both types of error increased with decreasing stimulus contrast, reaching a maximum of 27 ± 21% Miss rate and 9 ± 8% incorrect rate for single low-contrast stimuli on one side.
source: The probability of both types of error increased with decreasing stimulus contrast, reaching a maximum of 27 ± 21% Miss rate and 9 ± 8% incorrect rate for single low-contrast stimuli on one side (Figure 1h).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific error rates as a function of stimulus contrast, with data shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Optogenetic inactivation of visual cortex (VIS) biased choices away from stimuli contralateral to the inactivated hemisphere (−35%, p<0.0002).
source: Optogenetic inactivation affected the animals' choices when targeted at the visual cortex (VIS; light diffusion made it impossible to distinguish effects in individual visual areas Guo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019) and at frontal cortex (MOs; Figure 3a), biasing choices away from stimuli contralateral to the inactivated hemisphere (−35%, p<0.0002 in VIS, −22%, p<0.0002 in MOs; permutation test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific behavioral effects and statistical significance from optogenetic inactivation experiments.

claim: Optogenetic inactivation of frontal cortex (MOs) biased choices away from stimuli contralateral to the inactivated hemisphere (−22%, p<0.0002).
source: Optogenetic inactivation affected the animals' choices when targeted at the visual cortex (VIS; light diffusion made it impossible to distinguish effects in individual visual areas Guo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2019) and at frontal cortex (MOs; Figure 3a), biasing choices away from stimuli contralateral to the inactivated hemisphere (−35%, p<0.0002 in VIS, −22%, p<0.0002 in MOs; permutation test; Figure 3—figure supplement 1a–d).
evidence: The manuscript reports specific behavioral effects and statistical significance from optogenetic inactivation experiments.

claim: Inactivation caused no changes in the balance of Go/NoGo responses, no matter how strongly the inactivated region encoded upcoming action execution.

claim: There was no relationship between the strength with which a region's activity measured by widefield imaging predicted action execution (Go vs. NoGo choices) and the effect of inactivating that region on Go vs. NoGo behavior.

source: Correlates of sensory stimuli and motor actions are found in multiple cortical areas, but such correlates do not indicate whether these areas are causally relevant to task performance.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the manuscript's findings and previous literature.

source: Correlates of sensory stimuli and motor actions are found in multiple cortical areas, but such correlates do not indicate whether these areas are causally relevant to task performance.

source: Thus, sensory signals localized in visual and frontal cortex play a causal role in task performance, while widespread dorsal cortical signals correlating with movement reflect processes that do not play a causal role.

source: Neural correlates of sensation, action selection, and action execution have been found in multiple brain regions (Freedman and Assad, 2006; Goard et al., 2016; Hernández et al., 2010; Hirokawa et al., 2019; Liu et al., 2013; Park et al., 2014; Pho et al., 2018; Platt and Glimcher, 1999; Raposo et al., 2014; Steinmetz et al., 2019; Wei et al., 2019; Yang et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Widespread activity pervades the brain before movements.
source: A key confound when interpreting neural correlates of task variables is the widespread activity that pervades the brain before movements (Ahrens et al., 2012; Allen et al., 2017; Musall et al., 2019; Salkoff et al., 2020; Steinmetz et al., 2019; Stringer et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: The most common neural correlates of behavior appear to be with whether the animal will move at all, rather than which particular action will be chosen.
source: The most common neural correlates of behavior appear to be with whether the animal will move at all, rather than which particular action will be chosen.
evidence: This statement is supported by the manuscript's findings and previous literature.

claim: In a visual discrimination task, neurons in nearly all brain structures are modulated prior to upcoming actions, whereas neurons predicting which action will be chosen are rare and confined to specific regions such as basal ganglia, midbrain, and frontal cortex.
source: For example, in a visual discrimination task, neurons in nearly all brain structures are modulated prior to upcoming actions, whereas neurons predicting which action will be chosen are rare and confined to specific regions such as basal ganglia, midbrain, and frontal cortex (Steinmetz et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Cortical inactivation has little effect in some well-trained behaviors.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: In other simple tasks such as licking following a whisker deflection, performance is impaired by inactivation of many structures, including medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus.
source: However, in other simple tasks such as licking following a whisker deflection, performance is impaired by inactivation of many structures, including medial prefrontal cortex and hippocampus (Le Merre et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature.

evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Inactivation might disrupt the execution of the chosen action, for example, delaying it or reducing its accuracy, but not affecting the probability of the two alternatives.

evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to previous literature and represents a theoretical possibility.

claim: Inactivation might have no effects on the current trial, suggesting that the region's activity in the task reflects corollary discharge, redundancy with other regions, or cognitive processes that only causally affect subsequent trials.
source: Finally, inactivation might have no effects on the current trial, suggesting that the region's activity in the task reflects corollary discharge (feedback from other brain areas involved in action selection and execution; Crapse and Sommer, 2008), redundancy with other regions (Li et al., 2016), or cognitive processes that only causally affect subsequent trials (Akrami et al., 2018; Lak et al., 2020).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature and represents a theoretical possibility.

claim: MOs is thought to be critical for decisions based on sensory input from diverse modalities, such as somatosensation, audition, olfaction, and vision.
source: MOs is thought to be critical for decisions based on sensory input (Barthas and Kwan, 2017), from diverse modalities, such as somatosensation (Guo et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015), audition (Erlich et al., 2015; Siniscalchi et al., 2016), olfaction (Allen et al., 2017; Wu et al., 2020), and vision (Orsolic et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.
